_note: Beat scripts for the portfolio explainers. focus = [x0,y0,x1,y1] as fractions of the shot; say = narration; cap = on-screen caption.

beats.cap: One screen that opens your day
beats.say: This is how my day starts. The Command Center reads every system I run and tells me what is waiting, what is running and what needs a decision, before I have asked anything.
The snapshot is live: content waiting for approval, trades closed, the worst alert of the session, and the security position. Each tile is a real number from a real system, not a mock-up.

Underneath, it separates the work that is waiting on me from the work I have not published yet — content waiting for approval, tickets, support replies — so nothing sits finished and invisible. That gap is where projects used to die.
Track My Gold runs the YouTube channel for a gold prospecting brand. It has posted a hundred and sixty six videos and it is holding a hundred and fifty one suggestions that want a decision.

beats.cap: Approve, post or deny, one at a time
beats.say: Every suggestion arrives with the video, the draft comment and a category. I approve, post or deny it in one click, and a human is always the last step before anything goes public.
The same dashboard carries the search console, Instagram, the affiliate program and the tracking log, so the channel is run from one place instead of six tabs.
Gold Spot Explorer answers a prospecting question with public data only. Give it a latitude, a longitude and a radius, and it scores the ground before you drive out to it.
The map layers historical gold sites, active BLM claims, public land ownership and the USGS magnetic survey, so the score is anchored to what is actually under the ground.
It comes back with areas ranked by prospectivity and the named prospects inside them, and it tells you plainly which claims are open and which are already taken. No API keys, no fee.

beats.cap: Pick the agent, not the app
beats.say: Hermes Vision is the front door to a team of agents rather than one assistant. Each profile has its own voice, its own model and its own job, from marketing to risk.
Seven profiles, each with the model it actually runs: goldie on Gemini, fin and tradedeck on OpenRouter, dev on DeepSeek, default on a local reflection model. Pick the agent, not the app.

beats.cap: A frontier town, built in the browser
beats.say: Hermes Worlds is a 3D frontier town that runs in a browser tab. It is the same business model as the rest of my work, made walkable: a gold mine, a saloon and a forge on one main street.

beats.cap: Characters with a model behind them
beats.say: The characters are agents with a model behind them and a job to do, so a conversation in the town is a conversation with the same systems that run the dashboards.

Obsidian Brain reads the vault where every note, project and decision lives, and counts it: a hundred and twenty four notes, ninety five thousand six hundred wikilinks, and eighty three percent of the vault still unlinked.

The pulse panel plots new notes over the last sixty days with the seven day trend on top, so a quiet week shows up as a gap instead of a feeling. The insight list underneath names what was written and when.
Beside it, the tags and entities the notes actually hang on, ranked by count, so the vocabulary of the vault is visible instead of implied.
Applied Agentic AI is a twelve-module course on agent systems, multi-agent orchestration and deployment, written against the Virginia Tech and Simplilearn syllabus.

beats.cap: Module by module, a quiz behind each one
beats.say: The course runs module by module with a quiz behind every section, so progress means understanding rather than a completion checkbox. Sixty five hours and a capstone at the end.
The modules build actual systems: tool calling, retrieval, LangChain, planning and evaluation, each one landing as a runnable artefact instead of slides.

beats.cap: The portfolio you are looking at
beats.say: This is the portfolio itself. I built the generator because the work kept outrunning the write-up: a project was finished and the site still described the one before it.
The numbers under the headline are generated too: twenty six builds shipped, nine running now, ten agents and a hundred and twenty four notes in the vault, all read from the registry every build.
The consulting desk tracks the business side of the work: active clients, projects in flight, leads this month and revenue booked, all on one line.

beats.cap: Fiverr and Upwork in one pipeline
beats.say: Fiverr and Upwork enquiries land in the same kanban, so a lead from either marketplace moves through one pipeline with a next action on every card.
Below it, every inbound enquiry is logged with its status, and the lead magnet reports what it actually converted: a thousand visits, seventy nine downloads, nine enquiries.

beats.cap: A trading desk that shows its working
beats.say: TradeDeck is a multi-agent trading desk. The account value and the equity curve are read from the broker, so the top of the page is the account's own truth rather than a reconstruction.
Positions, realised profit and trade count sit next to the runtime that produced them. If the desk is not running, the page says so instead of showing a stale number.

beats.cap: Signals, risk gates and a runtime that reports
beats.say: Signals, the idea feed, the risk gates and the strategies sit behind the chart, and the runtime block says exactly what produced the number you are looking at. If the desk is not running, the page says so instead of showing a stale figure.

beats.cap: A shirt line that writes its own ads
beats.say: Peril Adventure Wear is a print-on-demand shirt line with a content autopilot. Posts per day, the drip schedule and the channel list are set once, at the top.
Each draft is a real shirt design rendered in three layouts and six print palettes, with the copy written for the brand: leave the place better than you found it.
Nothing posts on its own. Every draft waits here with its own status, and only an approved design goes to Buffer or to the shop, so the brand never speaks without me having read it.

beats.cap: Can anyone take this from me?
beats.say: IP and Competitor Watch asks one uncomfortable question of every venture: if this works, who already owns it? Six projects audited, fifty two competitors tracked, nineteen threats.

beats.cap: Ranked by how defensible it really is
beats.say: Each project is scored for defensibility, and the score is deliberately unkind: a local repo with no hosted remote cannot prove when it was built, so it does not get the benefit of the doubt.

beats.cap: Who is directly in your lane
beats.say: At the bottom it names who is directly in the lane, so I know whether I am early, late, or already a copy of somebody else.
Resmara is a product for estate agents. Send it one listing and it writes the brand guide, the fourteen day content campaign and the ad launch, which is the work an agent never has time for.
One credit produces a fortnight of posts per property: the brand guide, the campaign and the ad launch. It runs as a hosted service, not a prototype.

Project NOMAD is an offline internet: a Kiwix library, a local AI chat and an admin console on one small machine, so the reference material and the assistant keep working when the connection does not. This is the library.
Wikipedia, Wikivoyage, Wiktionary, Wikibooks and a full medical reference are all searched from the same page, served over the local network rather than from the cloud.
Token Killers is a free calculator for the question every team asks late: what is this model actually costing us? Ten thousand API calls a month, a thousand tokens each, on a standard model.
It bills out at eighty dollars a month, twenty four after the optimisation, and zero if you move it to a local model. Real published rates, no sign up.
Then the checklist, in order of what is worth doing first: prompt caching, a model downgrade, context pruning, batch processing, and the work you should not be sending at all.

This is my technique library. One hundred and nine moves ripped off my own instructionals, indexed by name. I type a position I keep losing and it finds the move, in English or Japanese, before I have finished typing.

beats.cap: Every move: position, Japanese name, timestamp
beats.say: Each row tells me what it is, which position it belongs to, the Japanese name, how long the clip runs, and the exact timestamp in the source video. No scrubbing through a two hour disc to find the four minute detail that actually matters.

beats.cap: Drill what you cannot hit yet
beats.say: The filters do the teaching. Guard, mount, side control, back, escapes, submissions, self defence, each with a count. Rip a disc, name the chapters, and the library grows. The clips stream off the drive on my desk, so nothing is uploaded anywhere.

beats.cap: Three numbers, one source of truth
beats.say: A personal ledger that answers one question accurately: what am I actually worth. Four hundred and forty eight thousand in assets, three hundred and twenty seven thousand of debt, and one hundred and twenty thousand of net worth, computed rather than remembered.

The accounts are grouped the way money actually sits: liquid cash, trading and crypto, retirement. Each group totals itself, so I can see that most of my paper wealth is locked up in retirement while the money I can spend is five and a half thousand.

Lines are entered by hand and marked as such, because a wrong number I typed is a mistake I can find, and a wrong number a scraper invented is a lie I will trust. The dashboard syncs the rest, and the page shows it syncing instead of pretending it is live.

An adult reading and spelling lab, built for somebody who is embarrassed about needing one. Two hundred and seventy four words are due for review and it opens with the smallest useful thing: a five minute session, not a curriculum.

Four tools do the work. Sound it out breaks a word into syllables. The sounds teaches the fifty three units of English. Spelling rules covers the magic e and the doubling, and their exceptions. Flashcards make the awkward ones stick.

Every day it puts one rule in front of me, like homophones, the ones that cost you credibility: same sound, different spelling, different job in the sentence. Progress is kept in your own browser, not on my server.

beats.cap: Autopilot on, engine idle, nothing invisible
beats.say: The Content Autopilot for Track My Gold, and the whole point is on one screen. The engine is on and idle, the eight step job is listed, today's one draft is done, two are waiting for review and one is approved. Nothing publishes that I have not seen.

beats.cap: One button, one draft, one approval
beats.say: Generating is a button, not a cron I have to trust. One draft or three, then dual approval: it can be signed off here or from Discord, and the same count shows in both places so there is nowhere for a post to hide.
